manifest.title:
Living in Switzerland: entry and residence, work and unemployment, social insurance
and pensions, health and accident insurance, taxes and household fees, customs,
housing and family, naturalisation and voting rights, and daily life - federal rules,
registering in all 26 cantons, and the procedures of the Canton and City of Zurich
manifest.scope_statement:
Everyday administrative life in Switzerland, for people who live here and for people
moving here, of any nationality: federal rules, how to register on arrival in any of
the 26 cantons, and the procedures of the Canton of Zurich and the City of Zurich.

Entry and visas: the visa duty, the visa types C and D, the 90-in-180-days rule, the
entry requirements, ETIAS and the Entry/Exit System. Residence permits and
registration: the Foreign Nationals and Integration Act, the free-movement agreement
FZA, SEM and ch.ch guidance, how to register on arrival in every canton and its
migration-office contact, and the Zurich procedures in full.

Work: losing a job, registering with the RAV and unemployment insurance. Social
insurance: what happens to the AHV, occupational provision and pillar 3a on leaving
Switzerland. Health and accident insurance: the insurance duty, premium reduction and
who is compulsorily insured against accidents.

Taxes and household fees: tax at source with its tariff codes and the Zurich rules,
the City of Zurich tax return and tax office, and the radio and television fee.
Customs: travelling and shopping abroad, ordering from abroad, declaring goods, pets
and plants, and moving household goods.

Family and home: family allowances and parental leave, marriage, renting a home, and
leaving the City of Zurich. Driving and vehicles: a foreign driving licence, vehicles
after a move, and City of Zurich parking permits. Naturalisation and voting rights.
Life in the City of Zurich: first steps, waste and recycling, dogs, kindergarten and
school holidays, integration offers and German courses, medical emergencies, and the
offices' addresses and hours. Waste collection in Basel and St. Gallen, and waste
hand-over in Lugano.
out_of_scope: Other topics: schooling beyond kindergarten entry and school holidays, the asylum procedure and asylum permits, social assistance, debt enforcement, finding a home or a job, and utilities.
Fees and appointment availability for any permit or office.

Annual quotas, the detailed procedure, forms, appointments and fees of an office or of a Swiss representation, processing times, documents beyond those listed on a covered page, the visa rules of an individual nationality (SEM's Annex CH-1 lists) and airport-transit visas.

Benefit amounts and individual calculations: tax tariff tables, rates and deductions, amounts of tax and refunds, pension amounts, insurance premiums and premium reductions, unemployment daily-allowance amounts and dog tax; every calculator.
The invalidity insurance (IV), the supplementary benefits (EL) and the bridging benefit.
Customs tariff numbers and duty rates per product, and the value or treatment of an individual consignment.

Beyond registering on arrival and the migration-office contact, cantons other than Zurich, and municipal procedures outside the City of Zurich except waste in Basel, St. Gallen and Lugano; federal rules still apply there and are served with a caveat.
Eligibility decisions for a specific person: the rules route population groups to pre-authored statements and compute no outcome.
Live data such as current processing times, appointment slots, job vacancies or insurer premiums.
Any country other than Switzerland, including German and Austrian rules that look similar.
Integration funding for municipalities and providers, and the refugee support system Integrationsagenda IAZH.
manifest.out_of_scope_response: Tell the user that this service does not cover their question, quote the scope statement, and do not answer from general knowledge as if it were grounded.
limitations: Every statement was written by an assistant reading the cited pages and checked against its cited excerpt by one named reviewer (`reviewed_by` on each fact); this is not a legal review.
Every fact was confirmed by the reviewer in the admin console's review queue, many in bulk groups; the review history is in LIMITATIONS.md of the repository.
114 English excerpts of cited federal pages stand next to the reviewed excerpts of 112 facts; no person has reviewed them.
English statements paraphrase the cited original-language text; they are not official translations.
Conditions route population groups to statements; they do not decide eligibility for a specific person.
Office addresses, opening and telephone hours and closing days are those the saved pages state; a location, channel or closing day a page does not list is not served.
Validity is unbounded unless the cited page states a date; freshness measures the age of the saved copy, not whether the page changed.

Some statements rest on a publisher's plain-language summary (priminfo.admin.ch, ch.ch); the conditions and exceptions behind them rest on the authority's own page or on the law, and every citation names which of the two it is.

For every canton the pack publishes the migration-office contact and registration on arrival: period, office, permit application, change of canton, online channel. Cover is uneven because the cantons publish unevenly, and a missing fact means that canton was not found to publish it. Anything else cantonal or municipal is served with a caveat. Most periods come from a cantonal statute; LIMITATIONS.md has the detail.

topics.title: Residence permits and registration
topics.description: Federal rules of the Foreign Nationals and Integration Act, the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons with the EU and SEM guidance, Canton of Zurich and City of Zurich procedures, the health-insurance enrolment deadline, marriage, and deregistering when leaving the City of Zurich.

topics.title: Cantonal migration offices
topics.description: The migration-office contact of every canton from SEM's directory.

topics.title: Zurich office contacts
topics.description: Addresses, opening and telephone hours, appointments and directions of the cantonal and City of Zurich offices the other topics name (Migration Office, Naturalisation Division, Road Traffic Office, Cantonal Tax Office, Office for the Economy, SVA Zurich, City of Zurich Population Office and naturalisation office).

topics.title: First steps and life in the City of Zurich
topics.description: The City of Zurich's newcomer checklist, dogs (city and canton), kindergarten and school holidays, school information in other languages, and medical emergencies.

topics.title: Waste in Zurich, Basel, St. Gallen and Lugano
topics.description: Zurich: Züri-Sack, collections, recycling, hazardous waste; Basel, St. Gallen: collection zones; Lugano: bags and ecocentri.

topics.title: Parking, vehicles and moving goods
topics.description: Blue-zone parking and permits in the City of Zurich; vehicles after a move and vehicle import in the Canton of Zurich; customs on household goods when moving to Switzerland.

topics.title: Tax return and household fees
topics.description: The City of Zurich's tax return and tax office, and the federal radio and television fee.

topics.title: AHV, the pillar system and retirement
topics.description: Who is insured by the old-age and survivors' insurance and who owes contributions, the individual account, the reference age and drawing a pension early or late, claiming it, survivors' pensions, coordination with other states, and a map of the three pillars (AHV/IV information service, SVA Zurich). The rules, never a pension amount.

topics.title: Social insurance and pillar 3a
topics.description: AHV refunds, AHV pensions abroad and pension fund cash payment on leaving, and pillar 3a (ZAS, BSV, Fedlex, Canton of Zurich). Unemployment has a topic of its own.

topics.title: Losing a job, the RAV and unemployment insurance
topics.description: Signing on with the RAV and an unemployment fund, the duties of a jobseeker, the daily allowances, interim earnings, insolvency compensation, labour-market measures, the end of the entitlement, EU and EFTA contribution periods, short-time work, the job-registration duty and notice periods (SECO, Canton of Zurich). The rules, never an amount.

topics.title: Tax at source
topics.description: Who is taxed at source, when the liability ends and the subsequent ordinary assessment (ESTV, Canton of Zurich).

topics.title: Foreign driving licence
topics.description: Driving on and exchanging a foreign licence, with or without a control drive (federal, Canton of Zurich).

topics.title: Health and accident insurance
topics.description: The insurance duty on arrival, exemptions, premium reduction and accident insurance (FOPH, Canton of Zurich, SVA Zurich).

topics.title: Naturalisation
topics.description: Ordinary naturalisation and facilitated naturalisation of a Swiss citizen's spouse (SEM, Canton and City of Zurich).

topics.title: Entry and visas
topics.description: Who needs a visa, the Schengen visa C and the national visa D, the 90-in-180-days rule for short stays, entry requirements, the visa application, ETIAS and the Entry/Exit System (SEM, FDFA, VEV).

topics.title: Voting rights
topics.description: Who may vote and elect at federal, cantonal and communal level, foreign nationals' voting rights, and how to vote in the Canton of Zurich (Federal Constitution, ch.ch, Constitution of the Canton of Zurich, Canton of Zurich).

topics.title: Family allowances and parental leave
topics.description: Child and education allowances, maternity, other-parent and adoption leave (FSIO, SVA Zurich).

topics.title: Renting a home
topics.description: Lease, deposit, notice, rent increases and defects (Code of Obligations, ch.ch, BWO); the Zurich initial-rent form.

topics.title: Customs: travelling, ordering from abroad and moving goods
topics.description: The value limit and the duty-free quantities when travelling, how to declare goods, what falls due on a consignment ordered abroad, returns and repairs, pets and plants, moving household goods and a vehicle, and taking goods out of Switzerland (FOCBS).

topics.title: Integration offers and German courses
topics.description: Integration offers and German courses in the Canton of Zurich, first information and counselling for newcomers, protection from racist discrimination, migrant associations and contributions to integration projects (Fachstelle Integration).

required_user_facts.name: arrival_date
required_user_facts.instruction: Ask the user for the date on which they arrive (or arrived) in Switzerland. Never assume the arrival date equals the first working day; people usually arrive earlier. Without the arrival date the 14-day limit cannot be computed.

required_user_facts.name: first_working_day
required_user_facts.instruction: Confirm the exact first working day; registration must be completed before it.

required_user_facts.name: employment_duration
required_user_facts.instruction: If unknown, confirm that the contract exceeds three months; employment of up to three months per calendar year follows the notification procedure instead: resolve eu-short-employment for it.

decision_rule.description: The binding deadline is the EARLIER of two limits: (A) 14 days after the arrival date and (B) before the first working day.
steps: 1. Obtain arrival_date and first_working_day from the user; do not guess them.
3. Limit B = registration completed before the first working day, i.e. at the latest on the last working day of the office before the first working day.

4. If limit B falls before limit A, tell the user to register before the first working day and name that date. Otherwise tell the user to register within 14 days of arrival and name the date of limit A.
5. State both limits so the user understands which one binds, and note that registration is only possible after the actual move-in.

notes: The German sample question was authored by the assistant on 2026-09-19 so that the concept has one in each query language (curation question_languages); it is not taken from the cited pages and not copied from a regression case.
Both limits apply together: the 14-day period is counted from the arrival in Switzerland, not from the first working day, and registration must precede the start of work.

facts.statement: ch.ch lists the foreign-national permit cards by group. EU/EFTA nationals: L (short stay), B (residence), C (settlement), Ci (residence with gainful employment) and G (cross-border commuter), each marked EU/EFTA. Third-country nationals: B, C, Ci, G and L, plus F (provisionally admitted foreigners), N (asylum seekers) and S (temporary protection). The free-movement agreement makes entry and residence much easier for EU and EFTA citizens; rules for other countries are more restrictive. The page lists the 27 EU member states and the EFTA states Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland.

facts.statement: SEM: residents (Ausweis B EU/EFTA) are foreign nationals who stay in Switzerland for a longer period for a particular purpose, with or without gainful employment. For nationals of EU/EFTA member states the residence permit is valid for five years and is granted on proof of an open-ended employment or one limited to at least 365 days. It is extended by five years when the conditions are still met, but the first extension can be limited to one year if the person has been involuntarily unemployed for more than twelve consecutive months.

facts.statement: SEM: short-stay residents (Ausweis L EU/EFTA) are foreign nationals who stay in Switzerland for a limited time, as a rule less than a year, for a particular purpose with or without gainful employment. EU/EFTA nationals are entitled to this permit when they can show an employment relationship in Switzerland of between three months and one year; employment of under three months in a calendar year needs no permit and is handled through the online notification procedure. The permit is valid for the duration of the employment.

facts.statement: SEM: a third-country national can be admitted only when no person with priority is available on the domestic labour market or on the labour markets of the EU/EFTA states. Priority is enjoyed by Swiss citizens and by foreign nationals with a settlement permit or a residence permit. The employer must make credible search efforts that show, in timing, geographical breadth and content, a genuine attempt to fill the post with domestic or EU/EFTA candidates, and should contact third-country nationals only after such efforts have actually failed. Posts are in principle notified to the regional employment centres (RAV), an advertisement in the European Employment System (EURES) is also necessary, and the authorities must be shown that the search through the sector's specialist recruitment channels remained unsuccessful.

facts.statement: SEM: the duty to notify vacancies is a further admission condition next to the priority of the domestic workforce. facts.statement: Canton of Zurich: the permit procedure runs in steps. The employer files the application for gainful employment with the Office for Economy (AWI); the AWI issues the labour-market pre-decision and forwards a positive one to the State Secretariat for Migration for approval; once SEM approves, the file goes to the Migration Office, which examines the application under immigration law and can still refuse the permit; if those conditions are met too, the Migration Office grants the permit to work. If the person is still abroad, the Migration Office authorises the Swiss representation to issue the visa by an entry authorisation, or, where there is no visa duty, issues an assurance of the permit to the employer. After entry the person registers in the municipality, where they are given an appointment to record their biometric data, appears in person at the Migration Office for it, and the card is produced and sent by post.

facts.statement: The Agreement between Switzerland and the European Community and its member states on the free movement of persons (FZA, SR 0.142.112.681) was concluded on 21 June 1999 and entered into force on 1 June 2002. Article 1 states its aims for nationals of the EU member states and Switzerland: a right of entry, residence, access to employment, establishment as a self-employed person and a right to remain; easier provision of services, in particular short-term services; entry and residence for persons not in gainful employment; and the same living, employment and working conditions as for nationals.

facts.statement: FZA Annex I Article 1(1): Switzerland and the EU member states allow nationals of the other contracting parties, their family members and posted workers to enter on presentation of a valid identity card or passport. No entry visa or equivalent may be required, except for family members and posted workers who are not nationals of a contracting party; they are to be given every facility to obtain any visa they need.

facts.statement: FZA Annex I Article 2(1): nationals of a contracting party may go to another contracting party, or stay there after an employment of less than one year ends, to look for work, and may stay for a reasonable period of up to six months where this is needed to learn of job offers matching their qualifications and to take steps to be hired. Jobseekers are entitled to the same help from the employment offices as that state's own nationals, and may be excluded from social assistance during that stay.

facts.statement: FZA Annex I Article 6(1): an employed national of a contracting party with an employment relationship of at least one year with an employer in the host state receives a residence permit valid for at least five years from its issue, which is automatically extended by at least five years. At the first extension its validity may be limited, but not to less than one year, if the holder has been involuntarily unemployed for more than twelve consecutive months.

facts.statement: FZA Annex I Article 7: an employed cross-border commuter is a national of a contracting party resident in one contracting party who works as an employee in the other and as a rule returns home daily or at least once a week. Such commuters need no residence permit; the employing state may issue a special certificate valid for at least five years, or for the duration of the employment if that is more than three months and less than one year, renewed by at least five years if the commuter shows they are working. The certificate is valid for the whole territory of the issuing state.

facts.statement: FZA Annex I Article 13: a self-employed cross-border commuter is a national of a contracting party resident in one contracting party who is self-employed in the other and as a rule returns home daily or at least once a week. Such commuters need no residence permit; the state concerned may issue a special certificate valid for at least five years if they show they are or wish to be self-employed, renewed by at least five years if they show they are self-employed. The certificate is valid for the whole territory of the issuing state.

facts.statement: FZA Annex I Article 3(1): the family members of a national of a contracting party who has a right of residence have the right to take up residence with that person. An employee must have housing for the family that meets the normal requirements for national workers in the region of employment; this must not lead to discrimination between national workers and workers from the other contracting party.

facts.statement: FZA Annex I Article 24(1): a national of a contracting party who does not work in the host state and has no right of residence under another provision of the agreement receives a residence permit valid for at least five years, provided they show the competent national authorities that they have, for themselves and their family members, sufficient financial means not to need social assistance during their stay, and health insurance covering all risks. The contracting parties may require the permit to be renewed after the first two years of residence if they consider it necessary.

facts.statement: The Central Compensation Office addresses nationals of the following states with a social security agreement who do not live in Switzerland: Albania, Australia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Brazil, Chile, Israel, Japan, Canada, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Kosovo, the Philippines, Quebec, San Marino, Serbia, Tunisia, Türkiye, the USA, Uruguay and the United Kingdom.

facts.statement: Switzerland concluded bilateral agreements to coordinate parts of its social insurance system, in particular the AHV and the IV, with states outside the EU and EFTA. Most of them cover several branches and contain coordination rules for benefits; a minority, the posting agreements, contain only rules on posting workers to the other contracting state and on the refund of contributions.

facts.statement: The bilateral agreements apply to nationals of both contracting states who are or were subject to the social security law of one of them, and to their family members and survivors. Nationals of third states are sometimes included, as are refugees and stateless persons with their family members.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages

facts.statement: Every bilateral agreement covers old age, death (survivors' benefits) and invalidity. Some also cover sickness, accidents at work and family allowances under the federal rules for agriculture.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: Added on 2026-09-22 from a page the catalogue already held; not yet confirmed by a reviewer.

facts.statement: The main effects in the AHV and IV are equal treatment of the other state's nationals, a single applicable social security law (as a rule the law of the state where the person works, with posting as the exception), and the export of ordinary AHV and IV pensions worldwide where the agreement provides for it. Ordinary IV pensions below 50 per cent are limited to Swiss territory, and some agreements provide for a lump-sum settlement, a refund of AHV contributions or their transfer to a foreign social insurance.

facts.statement: A claim for benefits is filed with the social insurance institution of the contracting state of the place of stay; an AHV or IV pension claim filed with the foreign institution is forwarded by it to the Swiss Compensation Office or to the IV office for insured persons abroad.

facts.statement: For foreign nationals with a settlement permit, a short-stay permit or a residence permit the insurance ends on the day of the departure from Switzerland reported to the residents' registration office, in every case on the day of the actual departure from Switzerland, or on the death of the insured person.

facts.statement: City of Zurich: Swiss citizens can apply for the city citizenship of Zurich when they have lived in the city without interruption for at least two years. The application needs the application form and, depending on the personal situation, further documents; it usually takes about three months and costs 200 francs, and is free for persons under 25. The existing communal citizenship does not have to be given up, because the Canton of Zurich allows several communal citizenships, but the applicant should clarify beforehand with the authority of their canton of origin whether several are allowed there.

facts.statement: City of Zurich: the application can be filed online or by post once all documents are together. Filing online requires a confirmed identity through an AGOV login, the official login for Swiss authority services, which private individuals can set up free of charge; the guided online submission takes about ten minutes with the documents at hand. By post, the form "Gesuch um Aufnahme von Schweizer Bürger*innen in das Stadtbürgerrecht" is completed, signed and sent with all documents. The Stadtkanzlei examines the application and prepares the request for the city council. Processing usually takes about three months and can differ with the individual case and the completeness of the documents; the fee is 200 francs and the procedure is free for persons under 25.

facts.statement: City of Zurich: furniture, mattresses, carpets, suitcases and wickerwork are bulky goods (Sperrgut), combustible waste too big and too heavy for the Züri-Sack. Metal shelves and other larger metal objects such as bicycles and grills are large metal; small metal such as tins, drink cans, small pans, screws, wires and aluminium foil can be taken to the recyclable material collection points free of charge. Garden shears usually count as large metal, with foreign material such as plastic or wood removed where possible, while small shears that fit through the container opening of 4 by 18 centimetres can go to the collection points.

facts.statement: SEM: an ETIAS travel authorisation is tied to the passport given in the application form and is valid for up to three years or until that travel document expires. With a valid authorisation travellers may enter the 30 European countries as often as they wish, as long as they do not exceed 90 days within a period of 180 days. The authorisation does not guarantee entry: the entry conditions are still checked at the border.

facts.statement: SEM: the EES is a system for managing the Schengen external borders. It records the entries and exits of third-country nationals electronically and calculates the duration of stay in the Schengen area automatically. The manual stamping of travel documents is replaced by an entry in the EES. The system is to make irregular migration, in particular overstayers, easier to detect and undocumented travellers easier to identify, among other things with biometric identifiers (facial image and four fingerprints).

facts.statement: Canton of Zurich: the tax-at-source tariff is written as a letter, a number and Y or N. The letter is the civil-status tariff; the number is the number of children who give a right to a deduction (minor children in the person's care or custody, and adult children in first education whom the person mainly supports, also when they live abroad); Y or N says whether church tax is due, which it is for members of the Roman Catholic, Christian Catholic and Evangelical Reformed denominations.

facts.statement: Canton of Zurich: the applicable tariff depends on civil status, children and denomination. A change that calls for a new tariff is applied from the following month: marriage, divorce, separation or widowhood; the birth of a child, a child's majority or the end of its first education; the spouse or registered partner starting or stopping work; a change of denomination.

facts.statement: Canton of Zurich: tariffs A and H are for employees living alone (single, separated, divorced or widowed), including those cohabiting with minor children under joint parental custody or adult children in first education, and those living alone with children whom they mainly support. Tariff B is for married employees or registered partners whose spouse or partner has no earned income or replacement income; tariff C for those whose spouse or partner has earned income or replacement income, also from abroad, since worldwide income counts.

facts.statement: Canton of Zurich, tariffs from 2026: the basis is the gross monthly salary. The tariffs are calculated with the cantonal tax multiplier of 98 per cent and, for the municipal tax, with the weighted average of the municipal tax multipliers: 116.00 per cent with church tax and 109.90 per cent without. The tariff is therefore the same in every municipality of the canton; it does not use the multiplier of the person's own municipality.

facts.statement: A person can set up and pay into a pillar 3a if they have an income subject to AHV contributions as an employee or a self-employed person. facts.statement: Pillar 3a is restricted retirement savings held with a bank or insurance company: a maximum amount can be paid in each year, interest is higher than on a savings account, contributions are tax deductible, withdrawal is subject to conditions, and a one-time tax based on income at the time of withdrawal applies when the funds are paid out. Pillar 3b is unrestricted savings such as cash, a savings passbook, life insurance or investments: any amount may be paid in each year, the saved capital must generally be declared and taxed annually, and it can be withdrawn at any time without an additional tax.

facts.statement: Family allowances are a form of social security and family policy meant to partly offset the costs of caring for one or more children; they comprise the child allowance, the education allowance, the birth allowance and the adoption allowance.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: The federal Family Allowances Act (FamZG), in force since 1 January 2009, provides a degree of harmonization but leaves the cantons room to set the level of benefits, the organization and the financing of family allowances.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: The child allowance is paid from the month of the child's birth until the end of the month in which the child turns 16; if the education allowance already applies before the 16th birthday, that allowance is paid instead. The federal minimum is CHF 215 per month, and cantons may set a higher rate.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: The education allowance is paid from the start of the month the child begins post-compulsory education, at the earliest from the end of the month the child turns 15, until the education ends, and at the latest until the end of the month the child turns 25. The federal minimum is CHF 268 per month, and cantons may set a higher rate.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: A birth allowance, paid for each child born alive or after at least 23 weeks of pregnancy, is optional for cantons to introduce and set the amount of; the cantons of Fribourg, Geneva, Jura, Lucerne, Neuchatel, Schwyz, Uri, Valais and Vaud pay one.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: An adoption allowance is paid once for each minor child taken in for later adoption, but not for a step-child adoption under Article 264c of the Civil Code; it is optional for cantons to introduce and set the amount of, and is paid in the cantons of Fribourg, Geneva, Jura, Lucerne, Neuchatel, Uri, Valais and Vaud.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Employees and self-employed persons are entitled to family allowances if their AHV-liable income is at least CHF 630 per month or CHF 7,560 per year; below that threshold they count as non-employed. Non-employed persons with modest income are entitled if their taxable income does not exceed CHF 45,360 per year, they count as non-employed under AHV rules, they are resident in Switzerland, and they do not receive supplementary benefits to the AHV/IV.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Only one allowance of the same type may be paid per child (prohibition of double payment). If several people are entitled to allowances for the same child, payment follows this order: the employed person before the non-employed person; if both are employed, the parent with parental custody; then the parent the child mainly lives with; then the parent working in the child's canton of residence; and finally the parent with the higher AHV-liable income from employment, or from self-employment if neither parent has employment income.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Special conditions apply to the payment of family allowances for children who live abroad.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Canton of Zurich: family allowances comprise a child allowance of CHF 215 per month up to the child's 12th birthday, then CHF 268 per month up to the 16th birthday, and an education allowance of CHF 268 per month from the 16th to the 25th birthday while in training. If training starts before the 16th birthday, the education allowance begins once the child is 15 years old and has finished compulsory schooling.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Canton of Zurich: employees claim family allowances through their employer. The employer's family compensation fund checks whether the conditions are met and, if so, informs the employer, who pays the allowance together with the wage.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Canton of Zurich: non-employed persons claim family allowances at the family compensation fund of their AHV compensation office; it checks whether the conditions are met and, if so, the AHV compensation office pays the allowance monthly.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Canton of Zurich: a non-employed person is entitled to family allowances only if their taxable income for direct federal tax is not higher than CHF 45,360, they are compulsorily insured and liable to contribute under the AHV, and they do not receive supplementary benefits.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Canton of Zurich: a non-employed person has no entitlement to family allowances if the other parent can claim them as an employee or self-employed person, if the other parent is entitled to unemployment daily allowances and thus also to family allowances, or if their spouse or registered partner has reached the AHV reference age.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Canton of Zurich: employees are entitled to family allowances if their AHV-liable income is at least CHF 7,560 per year or CHF 630 per month. If a person has several employers, the total earned income counts, and the company paying the highest wage is responsible for paying the allowance.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Canton of Zurich: family allowances can be claimed retroactively for at most 5 years; entitlement and payment are governed by the legal provisions in force at the relevant time.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: A person who is employed or self-employed is entitled to income compensation (EO) after the birth or adoption of a child if they have paid EO contributions for at least 9 months before the birth or adoption and were gainfully employed for at least 5 of those months; for an adoption, the child must be younger than 4 years old.

facts.statement: Employed mothers are entitled to a maternity leave of 14 weeks, which must be taken immediately after the birth and in one block. The maternity allowance is paid as a daily allowance of 80 percent of the average earned income before the birth, up to a maximum of CHF 220 per day; the maximum is reached at a monthly income of CHF 8,250 for employees, or a yearly income of CHF 99,000 for self-employed women.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: If a newborn must stay in hospital for more than 2 weeks directly after the birth, the mother is entitled to up to 8 additional weeks of maternity allowance, provided she continues working after the regular maternity leave; this extension is paid through the income compensation scheme.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: If the mother dies shortly after the birth, the surviving father, or the mother's wife if she meets the conditions for other-parent leave, is entitled to 14 weeks of leave taken in one block starting the day after the mother's death. If the father dies shortly after the birth, the surviving mother is entitled to 2 additional weeks of leave on top of the 14-week maternity leave, which can be taken flexibly like the other-parent leave.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: The other parent (the father, or the mother's wife where she qualifies) is entitled to 2 weeks of paid leave, to be taken within 6 months of the birth, either in one block including weekends or day by day. The allowance is 80 percent of the average earned income before the birth, up to CHF 220 per day; 14 daily allowances are paid for the 2 weeks, giving a maximum of CHF 3,080.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: The recipient of the other-parent allowance must be the child's legal father, or the mother's wife if she was married to the mother at the time of the birth and the child was conceived through sperm donation under the law on medically assisted reproduction. There is no entitlement to the other-parent allowance for an adoption; only the adoption allowance applies in that case.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Employees who take in a child under 4 years old for adoption are entitled to 2 weeks of paid adoption leave, to be taken within the first year after the adoption, either in one block including weekends or day by day (10 days). The adoptive parents choose which of them takes the leave and may split it between them but cannot take it at the same time; no compensated leave is provided for adopting a partner's child (step-child adoption).

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: The adoption allowance is 80 percent of the average earned income before the adoption, up to a maximum of CHF 220 per day; 14 daily allowances are paid for the 2 weeks of leave, giving a maximum of CHF 3,080.

facts.statement: A lease usually names the tenant party in writing (for a family home it is useful to also name the spouse; in a shared flat or concubinage all persons named in the lease are jointly and severally liable for the rent), describes the rented object (usually a flat, including rooms such as attic and cellar and shared use of areas like the laundry), and states whether the lease runs for a fixed term or an indefinite period, most leases being indefinite. It should also state the notice periods and termination dates and the monthly rent and ancillary costs; if the lease does not itemize the ancillary costs, they are considered included in the rent.

facts.statement: A tenant of a home or business premises pays a rent deposit (Mietzinsdepot, also called Kaution) only if the lease requires it; for homes the deposit is at most three months' rent. If the tenant provides the security in cash or securities, the landlord must deposit it at a bank in a savings account or deposit account in the tenant's name.

facts.statement: A tenant may sublet the whole flat or a single room, but must inform the landlord about it.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
provenance.source: Mietvertrag, Untermietvertrag, Pachtvertrag in der Schweiz. (https://www.ch.ch/de/wohnen/miete/mietvertrag-und-pachtvertrag/), saved 2026-09-18

facts.statement: The landlord may refuse subletting only if the tenant refuses to disclose the details of the subletting, if the tenant charges an excessive rent for it (for a furnished flat a surcharge of at most 20 percent may be charged for wear of the furnishings; otherwise the tenant should charge no more than they themselves pay, including ancillary costs), or if the subletting causes the landlord a substantial disadvantage.

facts.statement: For the rental of flats, the parties may give notice with three months' notice for a date customary at the place, or, if there is no local custom, for the end of a three-month rental period.

facts.statement: Landlord and tenant of a home or business premises must give notice in writing. The landlord must use a form approved by the canton that states how the tenant must proceed if they want to challenge the notice or request an extension of the tenancy.

provenance.source: Fedlex: Code of Obligations, SR 220, version of 1 January 2026 (https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/27/317_321_377/de), saved 2026-09-18
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: If several persons signed the lease, all of them must sign a notice of termination. In a family or a registered partnership, a tenant can give notice only with the consent of the other spouse or partner, even if only one of them signed the lease; a tenant does not have to state a reason for their own notice and should send it by registered letter to the landlord.

notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: A tenant who returns the rented object without observing the notice period or termination date is released from their obligations toward the landlord only if they propose a new tenant who is acceptable to the landlord, solvent, and willing to take over the lease on the same terms; otherwise the tenant must keep paying the rent until the tenancy ends according to the contract or the law.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages

facts.statement: A tenant has the right to learn the landlord's reason for a notice of termination, and can challenge the notice within 30 days at the conciliation authority of their municipality if it is abusive, for example because the tenant asked for a rent reduction or the correction of a defect, or because the tenant's family circumstances changed. If the notice is valid, the tenant is nonetheless entitled to an extension of the tenancy in cases of hardship, for example tight financial circumstances, illness, or the situation on the rental housing market.

facts.statement: A landlord may generally increase the rent if general prices rise (inflation), if the mortgage reference interest rate has been raised, if maintenance and operating costs have increased (for example administrative costs or property taxes), or if major conversions or renovations with improvements have been carried out.

facts.statement: The landlord must notify a rent increase to the tenant on an official form and give reasons for it; the increase must reach the tenant at least 10 days before the start of the ordinary notice period, and the landlord can raise the rent only for the next possible termination date.

facts.statement: The mortgage reference interest rate (Referenzzinssatz) that governs rent adjustments is 1.25 percent, valid since 2 September 2025; the Federal Office for Housing's page, saved on 18 September 2026, states that it remains unchanged from 2 September 2026.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages

facts.statement: If the mortgage reference interest rate rises by 0.25 percentage points, the rent can be increased by 3 percent; if it falls by 0.25 percentage points, tenants are in principle entitled to a rent reduction of 2.91 percent for that step.

facts.statement: To request a rent reduction, a tenant should send a request to the landlord, ideally by registered letter; the landlord must respond within 30 days and may accept the request and lower the rent, or reject it, or offset it against other cost factors while explaining why. If the tenant disagrees with the answer, or receives no answer within 30 days, they can turn to the conciliation authority, but must do so within 30 days of that deadline, meaning at the latest 60 days after the original request to the landlord.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages

facts.statement: A tenant can challenge the initial rent as abusive within 30 days of taking over the rented object, if they were forced into the contract by personal or family hardship or by the situation on the local housing market, or if the landlord raised the initial rent significantly compared to the previous tenant's rent, for example if the new rent is at least 10 percent higher than what the previous tenant paid.

facts.statement: Tenancy law distinguishes a severe defect (the home is practically uninhabitable, for example after a burst water pipe), a medium defect (the home remains habitable but its usability is reduced, for example a broken refrigerator), and a small defect (such as blown fuses, burnt-out light bulbs, or worn seals); tenants must generally repair and pay for small defects themselves.

facts.statement: At the start of the tenancy, a tenant should insist that a deficiency list (Mängelliste) is drawn up, ideally as part of the handover record. For medium and severe defects arising during the tenancy, the tenant should report the defect promptly and, if nothing happens, send the landlord a registered letter describing and photographing the defect and setting a reasonable deadline, for example 14 days, to fix it.

facts.statement: To marry in Switzerland, both future spouses must be at least 18 years old, have the capacity of judgement, not already be married or in a registered partnership, and not be related to each other in a direct line or as siblings.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages

facts.statement: A person without Swiss citizenship may need an entry visa for the wedding in Switzerland depending on their country of origin; the civil registry office or the Swiss representation abroad informs the couple which documents to submit, and after the check both partners fill in and sign the form 'Erklärung betreffend die Voraussetzungen für die Eheschliessung' there.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages

facts.statement: Once the civil registry office confirms that all formalities for the marriage are complete, the couple has three months to hold the wedding.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: The wedding may take place at the civil registry office of the couple's place of residence or, if they prefer, at another civil registry office in Switzerland; two witnesses who are of legal age and have the capacity of judgement must be present.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: The cost of a civil wedding (documents and the marriage act) is between 300 and 400 Swiss francs nationwide; special requests, such as a wedding on a Saturday, incur additional costs.

facts.statement: Same-sex marriage has been possible in Switzerland since 1 July 2022; no new registered partnerships can be established, but an existing registered partnership can be converted into a marriage.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 50 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-18)

facts.statement: Marrying a Swiss citizen does not automatically grant Swiss citizenship, but the foreign spouse can go through a simplified naturalisation procedure.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages

facts.statement: After the wedding, the new marital status and any change of name must be reported to the municipal administration, the cantonal tax administration, the employer, the bank, the post office, and insurers.

facts.statement: City of Zurich: to arrange marriage preparation, a couple where at least one partner has a foreign passport fills in the City's contact form, while a couple where both partners have a Swiss passport calls the Zivilstandsamt (+41 44 412 31 50) three months before the wedding date to book the appointment.

facts.statement: City of Zurich: both partners need good German or English skills for marriage preparation, including understanding what is said, asking and understanding answers to questions, and reading and understanding forms and documents in German or English; a partner who lacks this needs an interpreter (Dolmetschhilfe), which costs Fr. 165 and is paid directly at the appointment by credit or debit card or Twint.

facts.statement: City of Zurich: at the marriage preparation appointment, a Swiss citizen shows a passport or identity card plus a certificate of residence if living outside the canton of Zurich; a foreign national without a Swiss passport shows a passport or identity card plus proof of their residence status, such as a foreign nationals' ID (Ausländerausweis) or visa, and likewise a certificate of residence if living outside the canton of Zurich.

facts.statement: City of Zurich: for marriage preparation and the wedding, a person must be legally resident in Switzerland; without a lawful stay, such as a visa or a foreign nationals' ID (Ausländerausweis), a person cannot marry in Switzerland.

The page names welcome talks for newcomers, German courses and playgroups with integrated language support as examples of what many municipalities offer.

facts.statement: Many municipalities in the Canton of Zurich have contact persons for integration who also give advice on German courses; where the municipality of residence offers no such advice, residents can turn to the cantonal German-course advice, which is free and available in 16 languages. The canton also keeps a German-course database listing German courses and language examinations in the Canton of Zurich, and the page states that language examinations matter for the residence permit, for naturalisation and for education and work.

notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 25 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-22)

facts.statement: The cities of Zurich and Winterthur keep their own offer databases, which the cantonal page links separately: German courses and the moving-from-abroad pages of the City of Zurich, and the infoDesk / welcomeDesk and German courses of the City of Winterthur.

facts.statement: The Canton of Zurich states as an aim of its integration programme that everyone newly arrived from abroad is welcomed in Switzerland and informed about the most important living conditions and integration offers, and that personally conveyed and multilingual information is central so that newcomers can orient themselves and settle in quickly at their new place of residence.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages

facts.statement: In the Canton of Zurich it is first of all the municipalities that inform newly arrived migrants as soon as possible after their arrival about the local living conditions, give them a first orientation at their new place of residence and, where needed, arrange access to German courses and other integration offers. The Fachstelle Integration provides the municipalities with a guide for planning and running first-information offers, which also addresses municipalities that do not take part in the cantonal integration programme.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages

facts.statement: People with a particular need for integration support should be pointed to suitable offers as early as possible; the canton names three groups in particular: persons in family reunification, persons threatened by or affected by poverty, and persons with training and skilled-worker potential.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 25 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-22)

facts.statement: For further information, migrants can use the topic-specific counselling of the regular services or migration-specific counselling offers. The Fachstelle Integration provides authorities, institutions and private persons with a list of organisations that offer migration-specific and topic-specific counselling in the Canton of Zurich; the organisations on it show expertise in counselling different target groups and follow recognised quality standards. The Fachstelle updates the list at least once a year and states that it makes no claim to completeness; further offers can be reported to integration@ji.zh.ch.

facts.statement: The Canton of Zurich publishes information for a good start at the new place of residence on its page "Willkommen im Kanton Zürich", with links to further information and to suitable information points.

facts.statement: The Canton of Zurich describes racist discrimination as acts that demean people because of their skin colour, their origin, their language, their ethnic-cultural belonging or their religion, and names demeaning statements, exclusion, refusal of a service and violence as forms of it. It states that racism can be structural, can happen intentionally or unintentionally, can occur together with discrimination on other grounds, and can occur at work, when looking for a flat or at school; people with a Swiss passport can experience it too.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 25 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-22)

facts.statement: The Zurich counselling centre against racism, ZüRAS, advises people who experience racist discrimination. Counselling is possible in several languages and is free for people who live in the Canton of Zurich. ZüRAS is run by the Asylorganisation Zürich (AOZ) on behalf of the canton and the city.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 25 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-22)

facts.statement: Besides the counselling and specialist offices in the Canton of Zurich, the page names two further places for cases of racism in Switzerland: the reporting platform for online racism, where cases of hate speech on the internet and in social media can be reported (www.reportonlineracism.ch), and the counselling network for victims of racism, a network of specialist offices across Switzerland that advise in cases of racism (www.network-racism.ch).

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 25 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-22)

facts.statement: The federal Service for Combating Racism is responsible for preventing racism and coordinates activities at national, cantonal and communal level, and has published a monitoring report on racist discrimination in Switzerland every two years since 2012, available online since 2024. The Federal Commission against Racism advises, produces publications and carries out prevention, and its online legal guide explains the legal situation and includes a glossary of the most important terms. The foundation against racism and antisemitism GRA records racist and antisemitic incidents across Switzerland.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 25 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-22)

facts.statement: The Canton of Zurich names three legal bases for protection from racist discrimination: the Federal Constitution, which since 2000 holds as a fundamental right in Article 8 paragraph 2 that nobody may be discriminated against because of origin, "race", language, way of life or religious conviction, a right the Zurich cantonal constitution has held since 2005; the Criminal Code, which in Article 261bis punishes certain discriminating acts committed in public, including the public demeaning of persons or groups because of their "race", ethnicity or religion, hate speech and calls for violence against them, and the refusal of a service offered to the general public on one of those grounds; and the Foreign Nationals and Integration Act, which since 2019 holds in Article 53 that the Confederation, the cantons and the communes take account of the concerns of integration and of protection from discrimination when performing their tasks.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 25 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-22)

facts.statement: For discrimination on other grounds the Canton of Zurich names other offices than the Fachstelle Integration: discrimination because of sex or sexual orientation belongs to the Fachstelle Gleichstellung, and discrimination because of a disability to the Koordinationsstelle Behindertenrechte.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages

facts.statement: The Fachstelle Integration of the Canton of Zurich runs a platform for migrant associations on which migrant and religious associations active in the canton can be searched by various criteria, for example by municipality or region, and on which associations can register themselves. The canton launched the platform at the beginning of 2015 to strengthen networking and ease the flow of information, and states that migrant and religious associations inform, advise and enable exchange, mostly as voluntary work.

facts.statement: With the newsletter Migrazin the Fachstelle Integration sends information from the Canton of Zurich to migrant and religious associations; associations that want to receive it write to the Fachstelle to sign up, and earlier issues can be viewed on the page.

facts.statement: The Fachstelle Integration names a contact person for migrant organisations; on the access date of the page this was Deniz Yüksel, deniz.yueksel@ji.zh.ch, +41 43 259 25 27.

facts.statement: Under the cantonal integration programme KIP 3 the Canton of Zurich has up to 300,000 francs a year available in 2024 to 2027 for projects that concern people with a migration history and/or are (co-)developed by them, particularly when they also involve migrants who can take part less well in social life, for example for language or financial reasons. The Fachstelle Integration states that it will also support projects during the cantonal integration programme KIP 4 (2028-2032), with 31 October 2027 as the first deadline, and that projects addressed specifically to refugees have their own funding programme.

facts.statement: Small projects with total costs of up to 5,000 francs can be submitted to the Canton of Zurich on a rolling basis as long as funds are still available, and simplified rules for submission and reporting apply to them.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages

facts.statement: For projects with total costs above 5,000 francs, 31 October 2026 is the last possible deadline within KIP 3. The maximum contribution per application is 50,000 francs, the Fachstelle Integration examines such applications within two months, and only projects completed by the end of 2027 at the latest can still be funded.

provenance.author: assistant (Claude), reading the saved official pages
notes: review: confirmed in a bulk review of 25 facts (Alexander Bobrovsky, 2026-09-22)

facts.statement: The Canton of Zurich funds projects in two priority areas in 2024 to 2027: living together and participation, where projects are supported that promote encounters, the participation of migrants in public life and voluntary work in the field of migration; and dealing with diversity and protection from discrimination, where projects are supported that promote a constructive approach to social diversity and that develop and implement measures against discrimination and racism. Only projects that concentrate on one or both of these areas receive contributions.
